As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever must not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children is reinforced by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection. In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to study the provisions of articles 77 to 90, which already provide sufficiently severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this regional regulation for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295, namely 12 years. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigation and inquiry processes that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the prosecution and judge's verdict it is still light so it does not correspond with justice. I. GENERAL

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the scope of the household. 5. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or may result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because his or her parents or one of his or her parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. I. GENERAL

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in their respective regions. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

The principles of this Regional Regulation are principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, are actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having equal standing in the field of law and government. Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially stipulates that every person, certainly both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, certainly including women and children victims of violence. Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Whereas Law Number 1 of 1974 concerning Marriage, which in Article 1 regulates the definition of marriage as a physical and spiritual bond between a man and a woman to build a household based on Belief in the One and Only God. Article 30 stipulates that the obligation of husband and wife is to be faithful to each other, to love, to help. This Marriage Law regulates who is a biological child, as well as joint property, including how to continue its ownership or inheritance to children. If this Law is obeyed, it can prevent and eliminate Domestic Violence, unfortunately what happens in society is that Domestic Violence (KDRT) is increasingly rampant, precisely with increasingly complex modus operandi and causing increasingly horrific consequences. The principle of non-discrimination is in line with the recognition of human rights, therefore it is very appropriate that the Government of Indonesia by enacting Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), in Article 1 states the definition of discrimination against women and all its consequences if discrimination against women occurs. Basically work is only for adults, while children, namely people under the age of 18, are obliged to seek knowledge and play. However, due to the economic limitations of families, there are some children who have to work. Therefore Law Number 20 of 1999, concerning the Minimum Age Limit for Children to be able to work by providing provisions that parents and employers should pay attention to the provisions of this Law, so that even though children are forced to work, they do not lose their youth and can still attend school to ensure their future. Children who are forced to work are found in all regions, both in urban and rural areas. In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out.

As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever must not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children is reinforced by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection. In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to study the provisions of articles 77 to 90, which already provide sufficiently severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this regional regulation for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295, namely 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is already quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigation and inquiry processes that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the prosecution and judge's verdict it is still light so it does not correspond with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household sphere, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015, namely concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for the Empowerment of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for the Empowerment of Women and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warokhmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT);

From the provisions of the legislation above, we can understand how great the attention of the Central Government is to protect its citizens who are in an unpleasant position, namely when becoming victims of violence, but in reality the legal process is still rarely carried out for victims of violence which nowadays are increasingly numerous and complex in their problems. In addition, it turns out that the verdicts of District Court judges are still many that are far from the demands of community justice, including families and victims of violence. Hopefully with the enactment of this Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children Victims of Violence, in Musi Rawas Regency in particular, the handling, rehabilitation and reintegration can be carried out well, and the process of preventing violence against women and children becomes smoother, so that it becomes less and eventually there is no more violence against women and children. The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

1. Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is Musi Rawas Regency Government; 3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or may result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced unnatural or unwanted sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in contact with the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under the age of 18 years, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises custodial power as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental障碍 so as to interfere with his or her growth and development properly. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because his or her parents or one of his or her parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop the child in accordance with the religion professed and the child's abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Rights of the child are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so that they can live, grow, develop, and participate, optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in contact with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substances (drugs) abuse, children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will, is or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for self-strengthening and recovery of victims of violence. 33.

Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). I. GENERAL

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in their respective regions. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

RIGHTS OF VICTIMS

As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever must not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children is reinforced by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to study the provisions of articles 77 to 90, which already provide sufficiently severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this regional regulation for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in their respective regions. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

I. GENERAL

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in their respective regions. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

The principles of this Regional Regulation are principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, are actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having equal standing in the field of law and government. Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially stipulates that every person, certainly both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, certainly including women and children victims of violence. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. I. GENERAL

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in their respective regions. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

The principles of this Regional Regulation are principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, are actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having equal standing in the field of law and government. Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially stipulates that every person, certainly both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, certainly including women and children victims of violence. Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. This Marriage Law regulates who is a biological child, as well as joint property, including how to continue its ownership or inheritance to children. If this Law is obeyed, it can prevent and eliminate Domestic Violence, unfortunately what happens in society is that Domestic Violence (KDRT) is increasingly rampant, precisely with increasingly complex modus operandi and causing increasingly horrific consequences. The principle of non-discrimination is in line with the recognition of human rights, therefore it is very appropriate that the Government of Indonesia by enacting Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), in Article 1 states the definition of discrimination against women and all its consequences if discrimination against women occurs. Basically work is only for adults, while children, namely people under the age of 18, are obliged to seek knowledge and play. As a consequence of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia as a State that signed the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights is the answer. Considering that even though since Indonesia's Independence, the 1945 Constitution also stated the recognition of human rights as regulated in Articles 27 to 34, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence which is clearly a violation of human rights. In Law Number 39 of 1999 it is reaffirmed that women's rights are human rights (Article 45) and Article 52 paragraph (2), which states that the rights of children are Human Rights and for the benefit of children's rights it is recognized and protected by law even from the womb. This means that children are recognized as having freedom and liberty in accordance with their dignity as human beings, so that all forms of violence whatsoever must not occur to children, because it is a violation of Human Rights. The commitment and political will of the Government of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia to protect children is reinforced by the enactment of Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law

Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection. In accordance with the types of crimes against children that are increasingly occurring today, we need to study the provisions of articles 77 to 90, which already provide sufficiently severe criminal sanctions (threats). Examples related to this regional regulation for cases that occur in society are those that violate Articles 81, 82 and 83. For this reason, let us examine the contents of Articles 81, 82, 83 so that child victims of violence or sexual crimes in society receive legal protection in accordance with a sense of justice. Article 81 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence forcing a child to have intercourse with him or with another person, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp.300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp.5,000,000,000.- (Five Billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) also apply to any person who intentionally commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to have intercourse with him or with another person. (3) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 82 states: (1) Any person who intentionally commits violence or threats of violence, coercion, commits fraud, a series of lies, or persuades a child to commit or allow obscene acts to be committed, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 5 (five) years and a fine of at most Rp. 5,000,000,000,- (Five billion rupiah). (2) The Criminal provisions as referred to in paragraph (1) committed by Parents, Guardians, Child Caregivers, Educators or Education Personnel, then the punishment is increased by 1/3 (one third) of the punishment as referred to in paragraph (1)

Article 83 states: Any person who traffics, sells, or kidnaps a child for himself or to be sold, shall be punished with imprisonment for a maximum of 15 (fifteen) years and a minimum of 3 (three) years and a fine of at most Rp. 300,000,000,- (three hundred million rupiah) and at least Rp. 60,000,000,- (sixty million rupiah). These three Articles are very reformative Articles when compared with the provisions in the Criminal Code, which in articles 281 to 296 regulate provisions, where the most severe criminal threat is Article 295, namely 12 years. When compared, the Child Protection Law is already quite severe in establishing criminal threats and fines as regulated in Articles 81 to 83. The problem is, even though the Law has established severe punishment threats or sanctions, there are still Law Enforcement Officials who have not optimally applied them, so it is still far from reality, between law in book and law in action. In cases as regulated in Articles 81 to 83, Law Enforcement Officials often conduct investigation and inquiry processes that are quite heavy and exhausting for child victims of violence, but in the prosecution and judge's verdict it is still light so it does not correspond with justice. Violence against women and children also occurs frequently within the household sphere, even though we have had a law for 13 years, namely Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence (KDRT), but nowadays domestic violence is increasing in number. For the prevention and handling of domestic violence in Musi Rawas Regency, the Office of Women's Empowerment and Child Protection of Musi Rawas Regency has established an Integrated Service Center for the Protection of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency, based on the Decree of the Regent of Musi Rawas Number 703/KPTS/KPP/2015, namely concerning the Establishment of the Integrated Service Center for the Empowerment of Women and Children (P2TP2A) of Musi Rawas Regency. The Integrated Service Center for the Empowerment of Women and Children (P2TP2A) becomes a place for reporting, handling, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims of violence. If there is domestic violence or other violence that befalls women and children, it must be reported to the P2TP2A, but the existence of P2TP2A is not yet widely known by the community. Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, in essence is to realize a household that is sakinah, mawadah, and warokhmah, this can be read from the objectives of eliminating domestic violence, namely: (a) preventing all forms of domestic violence (KDRT);

Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

1. Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is Musi Rawas Regency Government; 3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or may result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced unnatural or unwanted sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in contact with the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under the age of 18 years, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises custodial power as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental障碍 so as to interfere with his or her growth and development properly. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because his or her parents or one of his or her parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop the child in accordance with the religion professed and the child's abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Rights of the child are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so that they can live, grow, develop, and participate, optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in contact with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substances (drugs) abuse, children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will, is or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for self-strengthening and recovery of victims of violence. 33.

To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

1. Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is Musi Rawas Regency Government; 3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or may result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced unnatural or unwanted sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in contact with the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under the age of 18 years, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises custodial power as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental障碍 so as to interfere with his or her growth and development properly. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because his or her parents or one of his or her parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop the child in accordance with the religion professed and the child's abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Rights of the child are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so that they can live, grow, develop, and participate, optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in contact with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substances (drugs) abuse, children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will, is or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for self-strengthening and recovery of victims of violence. 33.

I. GENERAL

The National Objectives of the Unitary State of the Republic of Indonesia, as stipulated in the Preamble of the 1945 Constitution in the fourth paragraph, are stated to include: (1) protecting the entire Indonesian nation and all Indonesian territory, (2) advancing public welfare, (3) educating the life of the nation and (4) participating in implementing world order based on: (a) independence, (b) lasting peace, and (c) social justice. To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. The Rights of Women and Children are recognized as Human Rights (HAM), which must be upheld and respected by all parties, but in reality there are still many women and children who become victims of violence. The commitment of the Central Government to protect children and women is reflected in the legislation below it. Regional Autonomy that is implemented has strategic value so that each region forms legislation (Regional Regulations), not only to express local wisdom, but also to become a guideline for Regional Governments to implement the legislation above it (the 1945 Constitution, and Laws) to address legal problems and social problems that occur specifically in their respective regions. This Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children is based on Pancasila and the 1945 Constitution, and refers to Laws that regulate the protection of women and children victims of violence, including Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women, Law Number 39 of 1999 concerning Human Rights, Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection as amended by Law Number 35 of 2014 concerning Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection, Law Number 23 of 2004 concerning the Elimination of Domestic Violence, Law Number 21 of 2007 concerning the Eradication of the Crime of Trafficking in Persons, Law Number 11 of 2012 concerning the Juvenile Justice System, Law Number 17 of 2016 concerning the Stipulation of Government Regulation in Lieu of Law Number 1 of 2016 concerning the Second Amendment to Law Number 23 of 2002 concerning Child Protection into Law, and other related Laws, Law Number 8 of 2016 concerning Persons with Disabilities, Supreme Court Regulation Number 3 of 2017 concerning Guidelines for Adjudicating Cases of Women Facing the Law,

The principles of this Regional Regulation are principles contained in previous laws and regulations, for example the principle of respect for Human Rights and gender equality and justice, are actually already contained in Article 27

of the 1945 Constitution, which essentially is a legal rule on gender equality and justice, while also reflecting recognition of human rights, because what is referred to as every Citizen certainly consists of men and women, having equal standing in the field of law and government. Also in Article 28 G paragraph (1) of the 1945 Constitution which essentially stipulates that every person, certainly both men and women, has the right to protection and freedom from fear. Article 28H paragraph (2) which essentially regulates the right of citizens to obtain facilities and special treatment to obtain equality and justice, certainly including women and children victims of violence. Violence whose victims are women and children occurs both within marriage and outside marriage. Whereas Law Number 1 of 1974 concerning Marriage, which in Article 1 regulates the definition of marriage as a physical and spiritual bond between a man and a woman to build a household based on Belief in the One and Only God. Article 30 stipulates that the obligation of husband and wife is to be faithful to each other, to love, to help. This Marriage Law regulates who is a biological child, as well as joint property, including how to continue its ownership or inheritance to children. If this Law is obeyed, it can prevent and eliminate Domestic Violence, unfortunately what happens in society is that Domestic Violence (KDRT) is increasingly rampant, precisely with increasingly complex modus operandi and causing increasingly horrific consequences. The principle of non-discrimination is in line with the recognition of human rights, therefore it is very appropriate that the Government of Indonesia by enacting Law Number 7 of 1984 concerning Ratification of the Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women (CEDAW), in Article 1 states the definition of discrimination against women and all its consequences if discrimination against women occurs. Basically work is only for adults, while children, namely people under the age of 18, are obliged to seek knowledge and play. However, due to the economic limitations of families, there are some children who have to work. Therefore Law Number 20 of 1999, concerning the Minimum Age Limit for Children to be able to work by providing provisions that parents and employers should pay attention to the provisions of this Law, so that even though children are forced to work, they do not lose their youth and can still attend school to ensure their future. Children who are forced to work are found in all regions, both in urban and rural areas. In order for children to obtain their rights, the socialization of Law Number 20 of 1999 is urgent to be carried out.

To achieve these objectives, in accordance with the doctrine of trias politica, there are three State powers, namely executive power for the administration of government, legislative power as the maker of laws and regulations and judicial power as the administrator of laws and regulations. In Indonesia, these three powers complement each other, for the implementation of clean and authoritative governance, from the national level to the regional level. The Republic of Indonesia is a State of Law (rechtstaat) and not a State of Power (machtstaat), so that all actions of its citizens, including those in the form of violence, committed by both men and women, are also regulated by law. CHAPTER II

RIGHTS OF VICTIMS

Article 1

In this Regional Regulation, what is meant by:

1. Regency is Musi Rawas Regency; 2. Regency Government is Musi Rawas Regency Government; 3. Regent is the Regent of Musi Rawas. 4. Domestic Violence is any act against a person, especially women, which results in misery or suffering physically, sexually, psychologically, and/or domestic neglect including threats to commit acts, coercion, or unlawful deprivation of liberty within the scope of the household. 5. Elimination of Domestic Violence is a guarantee provided by the state to prevent the occurrence of domestic violence, prosecute perpetrators of domestic violence, and protect victims of domestic violence. 6. Trafficking in Persons is the act of recruitment, transportation, harboring, sending, transfer, or receipt of a person by means of threat of violence, use of violence, abduction, confinement, forgery, fraud, abuse of power or position of vulnerability, debt bondage or giving payments or benefits, so as to obtain the consent of a person having control over another person, whether conducted within the country or between countries, for the purpose of exploitation or resulting in a person being exploited. 7. Victim of Trafficking in Persons is a person who experiences psychological, mental, physical, sexual, economic, and/or social suffering, caused by the criminal act of trafficking in persons. 8. Violence is any act that results in or may result in misery or suffering whether physical, sexual, economic, psychological to the victim. 9. Physical violence is any act that causes pain, injury, wounds, or disability to a person's body, miscarriage, fainting and/or causing death. 10. Psychological violence is an act that causes fear, loss of self-confidence, loss of ability to act, feelings of helplessness and/or severe psychological suffering to a person. 11. Sexual violence is an act in the form of sexual harassment, forced sexual intercourse, forced unnatural or unwanted sexual intercourse, forced sexual intercourse with others for commercial purposes and/or certain purposes. 12. Victim is a woman and child who experiences misery and/or suffering either directly or indirectly as a result of violence. 13. Women in contact with the law are women in conflict with the law, women as victims, women as witnesses or women as parties. 14. Child is a person under the age of 18 years, including those in the womb. 15. Family is the smallest unit in society consisting of husband and wife, or husband and wife and their children, or father and his children, or mother and her children, or blood relatives in direct line upward or downward up to the third degree. 16. Parents are biological father and/or mother, or step father and/or mother, or adoptive father and/or mother. 17. Guardian is a person or body who in fact exercises custodial power as a parent over a child. 18. Neglected child is a child whose needs are not properly fulfilled, whether physical, mental, spiritual, or social. 19. Child with Disability is a child who experiences physical and/or mental障碍 so as to interfere with his or her growth and development properly. 20. Child with excellence is a child who has extraordinary intelligence, or has special potential and/or talent. 21. Adopted child is a child whose rights are transferred from the environment of the authority of the family of parents, legal guardian, or other person responsible for the care, education, and raising of the child, into the family environment of adoptive parents based on a court decision or determination. 22. Foster child is a child who is cared for by a person or institution, to be given guidance, maintenance, care, education, and health, because his or her parents or one of his or her parents is unable to guarantee the child's proper growth and development. 23. Custody is the power of parents to care for, educate, maintain, foster, protect, and develop the child in accordance with the religion professed and the child's abilities, talents, and interests. 24. Rights of the child are part of human rights that must be guaranteed, protected, and fulfilled by parents, family, community, government, and the state. 25. Protection is all efforts aimed at providing a sense of security to victims carried out by family, advocates, social institutions, police, prosecutors, courts, or other parties either temporarily or based on court determination. 26. Child protection is all activities to guarantee and protect children and their rights so that they can live, grow, develop, and participate, optimally in accordance with human dignity and dignity, and receive protection from violence and discrimination. 27. Special protection is protection given to children in emergency situations, children in contact with the law, children from minority and isolated groups, children who are exploited economically and/or sexually, children who are trafficked, children who are victims of narcotics, alcohol, psychotropic, and other addictive substances (drugs) abuse, children victims of kidnapping, sale, trafficking, children victims of violence both physical and/or mental, children with disabilities, and children victims of abuse and neglect. 28. Service is an action taken as soon as possible to victims when seeing, hearing and knowing that violence against victims will, is or has occurred. 29. Victim recovery is all efforts to strengthen victims of domestic violence to be more empowered both physically and psychologically. 30. Implementation of Recovery is all actions that include services and assistance to victims of domestic violence. 31. Recovery implementation officer is a health worker, social worker, volunteer companion, and/or spiritual counselor. 32. Companion is a person who has the expertise to accompany victims to conduct counseling, therapy and advocacy for self-strengthening and recovery of victims of violence. 33.

From the provisions of the legislation above, we can understand how great the attention of the Central Government is to protect its citizens who are in an unpleasant position, namely when becoming victims of violence, but in reality the legal process is still rarely carried out for victims of violence which nowadays are increasingly numerous and complex in their problems. In addition, it turns out that the verdicts of District Court judges are still many that are far from the demands of community justice, including families and victims of violence. Hopefully with the enactment of this Regional Regulation on the Protection of Women and Children Victims of Violence, in Musi Rawas Regency in particular, the handling, rehabilitation and reintegration can be carried out well, and the process of preventing violence against women and children becomes smoother, so that it becomes less and eventually there is no more violence against women and children. Amen.
